body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of Cardiorespiratory fitness
Sustainable athletic performance is built on physiological adaptations like Cardiorespiratory fitness. When you align training load with real biomechanics, endurance and recovery improve together.

Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) refers to the ability of the circulatory and respiratory systems to supply oxygen to skeletal muscles during sustained physical activity. The history of CRF began with its establishment in the 1920s, followed by decades of ongoing research and development. Scientists and researchers use CRF to assess the functional capacity of the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. These functions include ventilation, perfusion, gas exchange, vasodilation, and delivery of oxygen to the body's tissues. Cardiac output also provides evidence of the body adapting to demands and physical exertion that it faces. As these body functions are vital to an individual's health, CRF allows observers to quantify an individual's morbidity and mortality risk as a function of cardiorespiratory health, measuring it using varying methods. Regular physical activity and exercise can improve CRF, thus decreasing risk of CVD and other conditions while improving overall health.
